title: Peace walks
hook: Maha Ghosananda leads peace walks across Cambodia after the killing years

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk in maroon robes who calls kindness his practice. Your line: kindness as practice. When someone frustrated you, did the words just like me come to mind? Day one thousand twenty-one.

A dirt road in Cambodia. At the front, a small, elderly monk in saffron, walking slowly, sometimes smiling, sometimes sprinkling water from a bowl on the people who kneel by the roadside. Behind him, a long line: monks, nuns, laypeople, some carrying flags, some barefoot. The fields they pass have seen terrible things. In some places there are still mines in the ground. Nobody in the line is armed. They're walking through a country that had been torn apart by its own government, and they're walking for peace. Today is the man at the front.
screen: `A DIRT ROAD, A SMALL MONK.` → `A LONG LINE BEHIND HIM.` → `NO ONE ARMED.`

segments.voice: His name was Maha Ghosananda, a Cambodian monk, and he was living abroad when the Khmer Rouge came to power. Under that regime, temples were emptied, monks were killed or forced to give up their robes, and Cambodians died in the fields and in the prisons. His students say his own family was among those lost. When the killing years ended, he went to the refugee camps along the Thai border. He set up simple temples among the tents, and there he chanted a verse from the Dhammapada that people say he repeated again and again. In Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." He was saying it to people who had lost everything to hatred. He didn't say it to excuse what happened. He said it because, as he saw it, more hatred would only start the circle again. Later, back in Cambodia, he began leading walks for peace, the Dhammayietra, a pilgrimage of the Dhamma, through regions where fighting hadn't fully stopped. People came out of their villages to meet the walkers with water and incense. Some walkers were hurt along the way. Still they walked. His way of putting it was plain: peace is made step by step, slowly, the way you walk. Each step can be a kind of meditation, and each meditation a kind of step toward peace. He didn't promise it would be quick. He promised it would be walked.
screen: `THE KILLING YEARS.` · `CHANTING IN THE REFUGEE CAMPS.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE DHAMMAYIETRA: WALKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: a short walk for peace. If you can stand, stand. If you can't, sit and feel your feet on the floor. Take one unhurried step, then another, at the pace of someone in a long line. If you're seated, just press each foot gently in turn. With each step, let one quiet word ride along: peace. Not as a demand, more like company. If your mind runs ahead to your list, notice it, and come back to the next step. There's nowhere to arrive. Only this step. The bell holds the time.
Peace walks. The Dhammayietra, Maha Ghosananda's walks through a wounded Cambodia, made one slow step at a time. Today's words.
Your line: step by step, peace. Today, take a ten-minute walk somewhere ordinary, and let each step carry that one word. Day one thousand twenty-one.

howItsDone: In Cambodia, the Dhammayietra peace walks continued after Maha Ghosananda, and Buddhists elsewhere practice walking meditation, sometimes walking together in silence for peace.

options: a verse: hatred ceases by love
fork.reveal: Maha Ghosananda set up simple temples among the tents and chanted that Dhammapada verse, not to excuse what happened, but to stop the circle.

original.note: Pali averena, 'by non-hatred', from the Dhammapada verse Müller renders 'hatred ceases by love'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a peace walk is a protest march.
what it means: a slow walk as practice, each step a kind of meditation, carried through a wounded country.
what a scholar hears: the Dhammayietra, a modern Cambodian pilgrimage rooted in Dhammapada verse five, where Müller has love for Pali non-hatred.
